In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms by which enterotoxins cause disease.
the role of proteolytic processing in the biological activities of cholera toxin, Escherichia col heat-labile enterotoxicity, and pertussis toxin.
the molecular mechanisms of action of cholera toxin (CT) and heat-labile enterotoxic (LT) enterotoxin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
trypsinolysing the A subunit at Arg-192 is not absolutely required to elicit cytoxicity but that it does enhance the biological activity of the toxin.
the cleavage at R192 in the A1 subunit of the heat-labile enter toxin (LT) does not play a role in the enzymatic activity of LT.
the trypsin-like modification of heat-labile toxin is not essential for the toxin to exert its effects but does enhance its activity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

trypsin cleavage of the heat-labile enterotoxic A subunit at Arg 192 is not essential for the enzymatic activity of the A subunits but is required for the toxin to elicit cytopathic effects in Caco2 cells.
proteolytic processing of heat-labile toxin is not essential for its biological activity.
proteolytic modification of the holotoxins of E. coli and Vibrio cholerae plays an important role but is not absolutely required to elicit the cytotonic effects of these enterotoxins.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the enzymatic activity of the A subunits of cholera toxin (CT) and heat-labile enterotoxic (LT) is not affected by proteolytic cleavages at Arg192, which is a residue that is located in the loop that connects the B and A subunits of the holotoxins.
proteolytic modification of heat-labile toxin at arginine 193 (192 in wild-type toxin) is not necessary for enzymatic activity, nor is it necessary for biological activity.

the enzymatic and biological properties of the A subunits of the cholera and heat-labile enteropathogenic toxins are not necessarily coupled, which suggests that they may have evolved from a common progenitor that acquired the ability to ADP-ribosylate the GTP-binding protein, Gsalpha, at different points during evolution.
